# HanVoice

> HanVoice (https://hanvoice.app) is a web app (installable PWA) for travelers
> preparing a trip to Korea. It teaches the Korean phrases you actually use on
> a trip and — unlike flashcard apps — checks that you can say them out loud:
> every phrase attempt is scored for pronunciation (overall, accuracy, fluency,
> completeness, per-word), and you rehearse real café / taxi / restaurant /
> market conversations with an AI partner that speaks Korean back.

## What HanVoice is

- Positioning: trip prep, not fluency. "Speak Korean before you land in Seoul."
- 13 lessons: 8 Hangul reading lessons (covering 21 of the 40 Hangul letters —
  the ones trip phrases need) and 5 Speak lessons of scored trip phrases.
- 5 Talk scenarios (AI conversation rehearsal, in Korean, with goals): order an
  iced Americano, meet someone new, order lunch at a restaurant, take a taxi to
  your hotel, haggle at the market.
- Pronunciation scoring on every spoken attempt (Azure speech assessment):
  overall / accuracy / fluency / completeness plus per-word scores and one
  actionable feedback line.
- Handwriting checks: draw Hangul on a canvas and get scored on proportion,
  stroke, and legibility.
- Free Seoul Survival Phrase Card: https://hanvoice.app/phrase-card.html

## Pricing

- Free plan: 20 scored pronunciation attempts, 10 AI conversation turns, and
  10 handwriting checks per day. Enough to genuinely start.
- Founder Pass: $69 once, lifetime access, higher daily limits (200 attempts,
  150 conversation turns, 100 handwriting checks). No subscription.
- Premium: $14.99/month, same limits as Founder Pass.
- Refunds: 14-day money-back policy — https://hanvoice.app/refunds

## Key pages

- Home / signup: https://hanvoice.app/
- Free phrase card: https://hanvoice.app/phrase-card.html

## Honest limitations

HanVoice does not teach complete Hangul (21 of 40 letters), does not promise
fluency, and is not a general Korean course. It is focused preparation for a
trip: being understood at a café counter, in a taxi, at a market — and reading
enough Hangul to navigate menus and signs.
